newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU fin mins to vet French vision of EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU fin mins to vet French vision of EMU.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, under growing pressure to restore confidence in the planned single currency, got their first chance on Monday to assess the new French government's position on monetary union.

France's unease with the stringent demands of the EU's budget stability pact, a measure designed to curb spending among countries inside monetary union, has raised doubts over whether the euro will be launched on schedule in 1999.

Arriving for the meeting, Irish Finance Minister Rauiri Quinn said he did not expect France's new finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn to offer more than a cursory explanation of the government's stance on EMU, which includes a greater emphasis on job creation.
"I think we'll get a clarification of a preliminary nature," Quinn told Reuters.

The budget stability accord, agreed by EU leaders after lengthy negotiations in Dublin last December, is considered an essential element of the euro's blueprint and is particularly important to Germany.

In a newspaper article on Monday, Jacques Delors, an adviser to the French government and former European Commission president, said Prime Minister Lionel Jospin favoured the stability pact but wanted a separate protocol included in the Maastricht Treaty which seeks to coordinate economic policies.

Bonn's demands for budgetary discipline inside EMU and its rigid stance on the Maastricht Treaty's criteria for membership has put it on a potential collision course with France's more flexible and critical approach.
Despite the renewed uncertainty between Europe's two political heavyweights, most ministers said they were confident that some form of compromise could be achieved.
"I don't think on the particular point of employment we will have problems because it is a concern of all the states," said Luxembourg's Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker.
Germany's own bargaining position is seen weakened in light of its problems in bringing expenditure under control and the recent internal row between the government and the all powerful Bundesbank.
The central bank rejected a government plan to revalue its gold assets in order to plug a gaping hole in Bonn's 1997 revenue stream.

The battle has left German Finance Minister Theo Waigel in a weakened political state, and many believe the episode might eventually force Germany to opt for a euro that includes a much larger number of initial members.
Yet on arriving for Monday's gathering Waigel was determined as ever to argue that governments must bring their 1997 deficits down to three percent of GDP -- the Maastricht Treaty target.
"Whoever says 3.3 percent will in the end land at more than four percent in other countries and that is not acceptable," he told reporters.
Other ministers were equally vocal in rejecting what they saw as a move towards a watered-down euro, one that would have less credibility in financial markets.
"I do not believe it's right to fudge criteria once they're established," Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, told BBC radio.
Monday's meeting, along with a Franco-German summit later this week, are seen as critical hurdles for EMU before EU leaders meet in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

The twice-yearly summit is expected to push through several important agreements on monetary union, including rubber-stamping the budget stability pact, which penalises governments running deficits above three percent of GDP.
